newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican teachers, police battle in wage protest.
newsitem.headline: Mexican teachers, police battle in wage protest.

text.p: Mexican teachers protesting against low wages battled with police as they tried to march to the presidential residence on Thursday.

Several demonstrators were injured and at least three were arrested after teachers belonging to an anti-government union traded blows and hurled rocks at riot police a few hundred yards (meters) short of the official Los Pinos residence.
Helmeted police drove the edges of their riot shields against women and children cowering against a fence in the midst of the melee, television images showed.

The march was called on Teachers Day, which is supposed to be one of respect for educators. The protest followed a rise of six percent in teachers' basic pay announced late on Wednesday, and a 10 percent benefits hike.

"It's an insult," Eduardo Valenzuela, a teacher whose head was bleeding profusely, said of the pay hike. "We have demands and look what happens." He said police rained blows on him after he fell to the pavement.
The Education Ministry said the new pay rise followed a 17 percent increase in January and was more than teachers got last year, even though inflation had fallen this year.
President Ernesto Zedillo, addressing a meeting of pro-government teachers, defended his education record.
"We are convinced that the best destination for Mexicans' money is education," he said.

As Zedillo spoke, the president of the lower house of Congress, Juan Jose Osorio, proposed a law mandating that eight percent of Gross Domestic Product be earmarked for education. It is currently less that five percent.
Protesting teachers, many hailing from the impoverished southern state of Oaxaca, said they earned on average less than $200 a month, which they described as "a misery."

"My students are also in desperate conditions," said Jose Antonio Vazquez, a teacher of 35 children in Oaxaca. "That's why we have to fight, to change the standard of living. But the government doesn't respond."

Some of the dissident teachers, members of the anti-government National Education Workers Coordinator, were allowed through police checkpoints to talk with presidency officials. Zedillo himself was once the Education Minister.

The marches clogged traffic in this congested city, and marked the second time in two weeks that riot police have been involved in pitched battles with protesters. Last week they fought against disgruntled policemen, in a scuffle that led to more than a dozen serious injuries and some 50 arrests.
